title: With desire I have desired (Luke 22:14–23)
hook: he longed to eat this Passover with them, and gives bread and cup
tomorrow: I am among you as one who serves

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger's upper room, furnished and waiting. Your line was make ready. What space did you clear for someone? Day five hundred seventy-eight.

Think of a dinner you counted down to. A first holiday home after a long time away. A table with someone you hadn't seen in years. You thought about it for weeks. When you finally sat down, you almost didn't want to start eating, because then it would begin to end. Luke says that's how Jesus came to this table. The room is ready. The hour has come. He sits down with the twelve, and before anything else, before bread, before wine, he tells them how much he wanted this.

In the King James words: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." That doubling, desire desired, is a Hebrew way of speaking that made its way into the Greek. It means very much, with all of me. I have longed and longed. He knows what's coming. And he wants to be at this table anyway. Then something that surprises many readers: Luke has two cups. First Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it among themselves. Then he takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to them, saying: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." And after supper, another cup: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Passover meals had several cups of wine through the evening, and Luke's two cups fit that shape, though nobody knows exactly how the meal ran in Jesus's day. Remembrance, in Greek, is anamnesis, more than a memory. It means bringing the past into the present. Here Christians understand the meal in different ways, and it's fair to say each plainly. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans and many Anglicans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Many other Protestants keep the meal as a holy memorial and a sign. All of them keep it, because he asked. And then the hard line: the hand of the one who betrays him is on the table. They start asking each other who it could be.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share a meal you've longed for. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've been meaning to eat with and haven't. Too busy, too far, too awkward. Picture the table: what you'd cook or order, where they'd sit, the first thing you'd say. Then think about what it would mean to tell them, at the start, before the food, that you've been looking forward to this. Not a speech. Just the truth. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. This week, set the date. The bell holds the time.
With desire I have desired. Jesus's first words at the last supper in Luke: I have longed, with all of me, to eat this Passover with you.

howItsDone: Christians keep the Lord's Supper, also called Communion, the Eucharist or the Divine Liturgy, in weekly or even daily worship in some churches and monthly or quarterly in others, repeating Jesus's words over the bread and cup.

original.note: Greek: with desire I desired. a doubled phrase in the Hebrew manner, meaning intense longing.

trapdoor: what you thought: the last supper, a farewell dinner.
what it means: a meal Jesus longed for, where he gives bread and cup as his body and blood and asks to be remembered.
what a scholar hears: the doubled 'desire desired' is a Semitic intensifier, Luke uniquely has two cups, and some early manuscripts give a shorter text of 22:19–20.

notes: Luke 22:19b–20 is absent from a few Western manuscripts (notably Codex Bezae); most modern editions include it. Mentioned only in the trapdoor. Confirm.
Four cups at Passover are attested in the Mishnah (Pesachim 10), which is later than Jesus; the script says 'several cups' and that nobody knows exactly how the meal ran then. Confirm.
Communion views summarized: Catholic and Orthodox (change into body and blood), Lutheran and many Anglican (real presence), many other Protestants (memorial and sign). Confirm each is fairly stated.
'Desire desired' as a Semitic intensifier (cognate dative): standard commentary. Confirm.
